posts.title: Sumrall restores hope as Texas faces a reckoning
posts.description: Franz Beard on Florida's renewed hope under Jon Sumrall, Urban Meyer's playoff concerns and the pressure on Texas. Photo by Chris Spears, GatorBait Media.
posts.author: Franz Beard
posts.html:
File photo: Jon Sumrall on the Florida sideline against Ole Miss at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium on Sept. 26, 2026. Photo by Chris Spears, GatorBait Media.

Thoughts of the Day | Oct. 24, 2026

A few thoughts to jump-start your Saturday morning:

Confession time. In the privacy of your own home with no one to witness, raise your hand if you thought two weeks ago that the Florida Gators would be most fortunate to limp home with a 6-6 regular season? Losing to Missouri and South Carolina in thank you sir may I have another fashion will do that to you.

Memories of Mizzou and South Carolina are in the rearview after the upset of Texas in Austin and the bye week has provided necessary time for Florida's walking wounded to heal up in time for the five-week gauntlet ahead. Have the last two weeks pumped hope back into the collective mindset of the Gator Nation? Or, is it because next up is Georgia next Saturday in Atlanta that you are tempering your expectations?

Fair questions that deserve honest answers.

Bunch me in with the doubters, especially after the way the Gators were skewered and rotisseried by the Gamecocks at The Swamp. Losing to Missouri wasn't necessarily a surprise given the way the Gators seem to always dial up crappy when they travel to Columbia. Even a 28-point loss could be rationalized to a certain degree. But blown out by the Chickens on national TV in The Swamp?

That had me thinking 6-6 likely, 7-5 if the offensive line could remember it's legal to block somebody wearing a different-colored shirt and the defense discovered that it is okay to get off the field on third down. Then came Texas and that 15-play drive that took more than eight minutes off the third-quarter clock. Once the Gators fell behind 17-3, the defense went beast mode, turning Arch Manning and the Texas offense into a generic version of corn flakes. You know the type. Crispy until the milk turns them soggy.

Hope is once again whizzing through my veins. Eight wins? Not only doable but an achievement since it will be doubling up on last year's four-win total. Nine? Not out of the question. Impossible without a win over Georgia or Kentucky but as Auburn proved to Georgia and Alabama to Kentucky, if you are vulnerable you can be had.

I'm not even going to think about getting to 10 wins. That would mean running the table but before dismissing that as a possibility, I can't overlook that Jon Sumrall had win streaks of 11 and 10 games in his two years at Troy, eight and five in his two years at Tulane. He is 48-14 counting the 5-2 at Florida this season. To paraphrase Curt Cignetti, he wins. Google it.

Some may dismiss this as another case of sunshine pumping on my part, but I started writing about college football in 1967. I've been around. Experience tells me certain coaches have this aura about them. I am reminded of the late, great Bum Phillips and his awe of Bear Bryant. Bum said, "He could take his'n and beat yours, and take yours and beat his'n." Wherever he was, whatever the circumstance, whoever his players were, Bear Bryant won. Something about Sumrall gives me a similar feeling.

I admit, I wanted Lane Kiffin. I think everybody did. All the things Lane says that cause us to shake our heads we would be defending right now if he were the Florida coach. He's only outrageous when he's coaching somewhere else. If he were a Gator we would be saying he's Spurrier, Part Deux.

But Lane is at LSU where he's probably going to win a national championship when all is said and done. Jon Sumrall is at Florida and I couldn't be happier. Starting with his first press conference, he's grown on me and continues to grow on me. He doesn't sugarcoat things. He speaks his mind. He demands accountability from his coaches, his players and everyone associated with the program. He takes personal responsibility when everyone else around him comes up short of expectations.

I think he's the right coach at the right time and for all any of us know, he just might win a national championship here before Lane Kiffin wins one at LSU. Wouldn't that be a hoot?

URBAN MEYER ON THE FLAW IN THE 24-TEAM PLAYOFF

Like it or not – I don't – the 24-team College Football Playoff era is upon us, maybe as soon as next year. I may warm to the eventuality of playoff expansion but for now I'm stuck in the Stone Age.

Urban Meyer, while admitting the 24-team playoff concept has grown on him to the point of acceptance, laments that expansion isn't without consequences.

On his Triple Option podcast, Meyer said, "The only concern I have, and I'll keep saying this as long as I'm around, those who say that conference championship games are not important, I will say never played in it, never coached in it, and never won a ring … Conference championship games are one of the most exciting things that ever happened in my lifetime, and certainly for my players. And they're gone. They're gone."

ONE FINAL PITHY THOUGHT

Texas athletic director Chris Del Conte spent a portion of his Friday trying to convince the civilized world that everything is just peachy on The 40 Acres, which is what Texas calls the campus in Austin. Sark is just fine. Arch couldn't be better. Life could be a dream. The only people who don't think so are the ones who don't live in Austin.

He was selling hard. Not so sure how many are buying, certainly not those of us living in the real world. And how many of the folks living in Austin are happy that, despite all the cold, hard cash the faithful have poured into football, the Longhorns find themselves on the brink of playoff elimination?

Life could be a dream is the Del Conte message and yes, should the Longhorns whip up on Ole Miss tonight and run the rest of the regular season table they will be sitting pretty at 10-2, virtually assured of the College Football Playoff. Do that and Steve Sarkisian goes from overhyped and time to leave to conquering hero who should hang around awhile.

Nightmares are dreams, too. If you ignore the peachy keen rhetoric, instead taking the I live in the real world approach, a nightmare is what Texas will have if it gets kicked in the crotch by Ole Miss tonight. Thanks to the Big 12 which could have two unbeatens and another two one-loss teams in the regular season, the Southeastern Conference probably only gets three teams in the playoff, none of which will have three losses. So tonight is an elimination game for the Longhorns.

As if the idea of missing the playoff isn't pressure enough, there is the Manning factor. Ole Miss is where Archie and Eli Manning played college football. The entire Manning clan with the exception of Peyton, who the faithful whisper was dropped on his head too many times as an infant, thus explaining why he went to Tennessee, is Ole Miss royalty. Texas has to win this game for obvious reasons, but Arch Manning has to play lights out to uphold the Manning honor. If Arch flames out like he did against Oklahoma and Florida, it will be like tossing a couple of those NASCAR pitstop cans filled with gas on the bonfire that is already raging back in Austin.

Here is the kicker to this narrative. Had Arch chosen Ole Miss instead of Texas back when he was the consensus No. 1 high school quarterback in the country, it is highly unlikely that Trinidad Chambliss would have wound up in Oxford. Trinidad is the nation's best quarterback, whose journey to Ole Miss is routed through Division II Ferris State in Michigan. On his average to bad days he's still better than Arch is on his good ones. On his good days, Trinidad Chambliss performs like it's a Heisman Trophy audition. With him at QB, Ole Miss might win the national championship. He's that good.

Would Arch have developed at Ole Miss? He certainly hasn't developed under Steve Sarkisian who seems destined for a pink slip in the event of a loss tonight. The next and most painful question that begs to be asked: Is Arch Manning simply the worst of the Manning quarterbacks? Secondly, can his career be rehabbed?

If Sark loses tonight everything won't be peachy in Burnt Orange Country. If you believe the rumblings from the boosters that echo from sea to shining sea, Sark is a goner if he loses to Ole Miss. The last two games have exposed Arch's lack of football common sense. His inconsistent football instincts are why he has gone from a candidate to be the overall No. 1 draft pick next April to desperately needs another year of college football to see if the rough edges can be smoothed out. Will he stay at Texas if Sark is fired? Ole Miss will need a QB next year. As blasphemous as it sounds, would Ole Miss even welcome Arch if he entered the portal?

This is football's version of the soap opera. If Days of Our Lives had plots like this it would still be on network TV instead of streaming.

posts.title: Florida-Georgia outlook and SEC picks
posts.description: Franz Beard on Florida’s bye-week recovery before Georgia, six SEC matchups and the NCAA’s latest eligibility fight.
posts.author: Franz Beard
posts.html:
Vernell Brown III at The Swamp, and Tramell Jones Jr. handing off to Jadan Baugh against Texas in Austin. Brown photo by Chris Spears, GatorBait Media; Jones/Baugh photo courtesy UAA and Hannah White. Editorial collage by GatorBait Media.

Thoughts of the Day · October 23, 2026

A few thoughts to jump start your Friday morning:

Traditionally, both Florida and Georgia have a bye week prior to their close encounter, usually in Jacksonville but in Atlanta this year, Tampa next while EverBank Stadium is renovated. No one could have possibly foreseen just how perfect the timing of the bye week would be for Jon Sumrall, whose 20th-ranked Gators (5-2, 3-2 SEC) have used the open date to heal their banged up wide receiver corps. Getting Vernell Brown III, Eric Singleton Jr. and Bailey Stockton as close to full speed as possible enhances the Gators' chances to spring the upset on the 5th-ranked Bulldogs (6-1, 4-1 SEC), who were exposed as vulnerable by Auburn, a team the Gators beat.

The extra week also benefits Florida quarterback Aaron Philo, who took a blow to his throwing shoulder in the loss to South Carolina and missed the Gators' upset of Texas. It is said to be either a bruised or sprained AC joint. Best-case scenario for healing: three to four weeks. Worst case, out the rest of the year. The game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta will be week three in the healing process. Enough time for Philo to be healthy enough to play? Only time will answer that question.

Meanwhile, Tramell Jones Jr. has a Texas scalp under his belt and he's preparing in earnest to earn his spot in Gator lore if he's able to take down a second top-10 team in just his second start. He rallied the Gators from 14 down to win against that fierce Texas defense and he did it without Brown and with Singleton and Stockton both slowed by injuries.

Whether it's Philo or Jones taking the snaps, if all the receivers are at or near 100 percent the idea that the Gators could beat Georgia doesn't seem as preposterous an idea as it might have only a few weeks ago.

THE SEC SOOTHSAYER

No. 7 Ole Miss (5-1, 3-1 SEC) at No. 19 Texas (4-2, 1-2 SEC)

7:30 p.m., ABC

This could one day be known as Sark's Last Stand. Lose and the Longhorns, for all practical purposes, are left sitting on the curb while a whole bunch of College Football Playoff contenders go whizzing by. Lose, and for all practical purposes, Steve Sarkisian is a dead man walking.

Texas lost to Florida and a backup QB making his first collegiate start last week.

This week the Longhorns get to face probably the best college football quarterback in the country in Trinidad Chambliss, who has the luxury once again of handing the ball off to Kewan Lacy, finally healthy and running over, under, around and through people.

Texas has to hope that Arch Manning will be inspired by the idea of beating the alma mater of Hall of Fame relatives, grandfather Archie and uncle Eli. The Ole Miss defense just held Missouri to a three-spot. The Rebels are good enough to win this one by a couple of touchdowns if they don't turn the ball over.

The Sayer Says Sooth!: Here's something to rattle around in your brains. Ole Miss wins, Sark gets fired and at the end of the season, Arch hears Mama call and transfers to Ole Miss where he can get coached up (finally!) and restore the honor of the Manning name. Texas is somehow a 3.5-point favorite. It's not because of Arch but because of Will Muschamp's defense. Doesn't matter. Ole Miss is going to emerge the winner.

No. 11 Tennessee (6-1, 3-1 SEC) at South Carolina (3-3, 1-3 SEC)

3:30 p.m., ESPN

Something seems very wrong here. The Vols are coming off a dominant 25-10 win over Alabama, a no doubter if ever there was one. Yet, here we are a week later and they're 2.5-point underdogs on the road at Willy Brice where the Chickens had a bye week.

Do the experts think LaNorris Sellers awakened from a coma when he led South Carolina to a decisive win over Florida in The Swamp? That's what it will take for South Carolina to win this one, but if they do stick it to the Vols, it is very likely Shane Beamer will be coaching in Columbia again next year.

When the Chickens beat Florida, they stuffed the run and made the Florida passing game very ordinary. Something along those lines will be necessary along with Sellers escaping the UT pass rush, which leads the nation with 30 sacks.

Can the Vols run the football? If they can't they're going to lose.

The Sayer Says Sooth!: It's really tempting to pick an upset here but the way Tennessee played last week against Alabama says no way. However, if it is close at the end of the third quarter, all bets are off.

Vanderbilt (3-4, 0-4 SEC) at No. 12 Kentucky (6-1, 4-1 SEC)

7:30 p.m., SEC Network

The way Will Stein has the Wildcats playing, the UK faithful need to be ordering Ted Lasso "Believe" T-shirts and sweatshirts in bulk. If Kentucky beats Vanderbilt Saturday evening, the Wildcats will have guaranteed their first winning season since 2023.

For all the talk about how Stein has rejuvenated the UK offense, it's the defense that is actually stealing the show. The Wildcats lead the SEC in turnover margin. Vanderbilt is learning what life is like with a true freshman quarterback in the SEC. Jared Curtis is going to be a fine quarterback someday. Just not Saturday.

Vandy fans must be wondering how it is that Kentucky basketball player Franck Kepnang got a seventh year from the NCAA and Diego Pavia didn't get a seventh (or is it eighth) to play football at Vanderbilt? The Commodores are a 10.5-point underdog in Lexington. It feels like that number is way too small.

The Sayer Says Sooth!: A win would certainly change the mood on Nashville's West End where folks are thinking we're back to being Vandy again after winning 10 games last year. The Commodores will be fortunate to find another win on their schedule, so 3-9 is highly likely. Something about this one says Kentucky wins in a blowout.

Texas A&M (4-3, 1-3 SEC) at No. 13 Alabama (5-2, 3-2 SEC)

3:30 p.m., ABC

Is there a more disappointing team in the SEC than the Aggies? And, is there a more disappointing QB in the entire country than Marcel Reed? With that being said, this is a chance for both the Aggies and Reed to right a listing ship. Can they spring the upset? A week ago the answer would have been no, not a chance and hell no.

That was before Alabama got thoroughly exposed by Tennessee's defense which sacked Keelon Russell five times, held the Tide to 54 rushing yards, forced four turnovers and allowed only 10 points.

Mike Elko's rep is that of a defensive genius. Can he get the Aggies to replicate what Tennessee did? Can Marcel Reed remember it's not nice to turn the ball over?

As for Alabama, this is an elimination game, for the team's hopes of the College Football Playoff and perhaps for Kalen DeBoer's hopes of being gainfully employed in Tuscaloosa next year. A third loss this season will be his eleventh in three years. Bama fans are quick to tell you Nick never did that.

The Sayer Says Sooth!: This just reeks of an upset even though the Aggies have found themselves on the blowout end of two of their three SEC losses. The Aggies are 13.5-point underdogs and Alabama will be without its most explosive offensive player, wide receiver Ryan Coleman-Williams. If Alabama still has a Tennessee hangover, it will be low tide in Tuscaloosa. Fortunately for Alabama, Marcel Reed is the opposing QB, but it's going to be a chest clutcher at the end.

No. 18 LSU (5-2, 2-2 SEC) at Auburn (4-2, 2-2 SEC)

12 noon, ABC

This may turn out to be the best game of the day. LSU's defense pitched a shutout last week at Mississippi State while Auburn QB Byrum Brown was too hot for Georgia to handle in Athens. LSU is giving up only 88 yards per game on the ground and has sacked quarterbacks 27 times.

Sam Leavitt is starting to play like the QB he was hyped to be when he transferred in from Arizona State. None of that bodes well for Auburn, which ranks dead last in the SEC and 134th nationally in sacks allowed.

Florida sacked Brown seven times. Georgia got to Brown five times last week, but he escaped enough times to lead Auburn to a shocking win.

He needs to be in his feets don't fail me now mode against LSU and Auburn's defense needs to play as well as it did last week when it forced three critical Georgia turnovers.

The Sayer Says Sooth!: It's an elimination game for LSU, which has to win the next five games to have a shot at the College Football Playoff. For Auburn, it's a chance to prove the win over Georgia wasn't a fluke and that first-year coach Alex Golesh has the Tigers headed onward and upward. Lane Kiffin knows what it takes to motivate a team when its back is to the wall. LSU is favored by a TD. White knuckles at the end and Lane gets a win.

Oklahoma (3-3, 1-2 SEC) at Mississippi State (4-2, 2-2 SEC)

3:30 p.m., SEC Network

Oklahoma is sticking with John Mateer at quarterback. If Kamario Taylor and Fluff Bothwell can't go for Mississippi State, Mateer might be the Bulldogs' secret weapon due to his penchant for completing passes to the other team.

Oklahoma has a world-class defense that held Kentucky to 230 yards last week. If Mateer and the offense had cooperated, the Sooners would have won the game.

Without Taylor and Bothwell, Mississippi State's offense is on the same plane as Oklahoma.

The Sayer Says Sooth!: Oklahoma is a 5.5-point favorite, largely due to the likelihood Taylor and Bothwell won't play. The Bulldogs are an explosive team with their two studs. Without them, they will go down in what promises to be an ugly game from start to finish.

ONE FINAL PITHY THOUGHT

There is a theory out there, most recently promoted by Arizona basketball coach Tommy Lloyd and embraced by Gary Parrish of CBS, the best basketball writer in the country, that the NCAA is actually promoting the chaos that it claims will result from 2022 high school grads getting a fifth year of eligibility. Bear with me on this one. It's complicated but logical.

It goes something like this: The NCAA, in its infinite wisdom, claims that 2022 high school grads are excluded from a fifth year of eligibility because (a) it will create fewer opportunities for incoming freshmen and (b) a coach adding a 2022 grad to his roster will in turn cut a player already on scholarship. Therefore, chaos! Florida coach Todd Golden debunked that defense more than a week ago.

Meanwhile, 2022 athletes who feel unfairly left out by the NCAA have taken to the courts where they are winning injunctions that will make them eligible. The NCAA is appealing their injunctions and in some cases getting a stay of the players' temporary restraining orders. Millions of billable hours for attorneys and players' lives held hostage.

The NCAA, of course, could give up the appeals and simply grandfather the players in, making them eligible to play. So why doesn't that happen? This is where Lloyd and Parrish chime in – it is because the NCAA is trying to create the chaos it claims to be fighting for the purpose of taking a cattle prod to Congress to pass the Protect College Sports Act.

"I think my theory is this thing has gotten so political – and, obviously, there are a lot of things that need to be fixed in college sports," Lloyd said. "So [in my opinion,] the NCAA doesn't mind the 'chaos' right now because it can help drive the case for them to promote the [Protect] College Sports Act, which I'm sure we need."

Translation: The NCAA is so out of control it needs an act of Congress to stabilize things and it's willing to sacrifice the players it claims to protect to get the outside help it HOPES will save its control.

What we really need is something other than the NCAA, but unfortunately no one has a Plan B for a brand new organization that will enforce its own rules fairly.

posts.title: From The Scout Team To Atlanta: Chris Doering Finally Gets His Due
posts.description: Buddy Martin looks back at Chris Doering's path from walk-on to Florida's record-setting receiver and the recognition that followed.
posts.author: Buddy Martin
posts.html:
He left in 1995 with 31 touchdown catches, still the school record and second in SEC history. Think about the receivers who have come through Gainesville since then

By Buddy Martin

They used to hand Chris Doering a scout-team jersey and tell him to go get hit. He'd take the beating, show up the next day, and take it again. No scholarship or promise came with it, and nobody in Gainesville was printing his name in the program.

He was a skinny kid from P.K. Yonge whose dream was bigger than his resume. Thirty-five years later, that kid is an SEC Legend. Doering was named Thursday last week to the 2026 SEC Football Legends class.

It's a 16-member group full of Heisman Trophy winners, national champions and NFL stars: Nick Saban of Alabama, Mark Richt of Georgia, Billy Sims of Oklahoma, Patrick Peterson of LSU, Randall Cobb of Kentucky and Ricky Williams of Texas.

The walk-on is standing in that crowd. Tell me this game doesn't still make room for a good story.

"The Scarlet Letter"

You have to understand how much that label stung. "I hated being called a walk-on," Doering told me on The Buddy Martin Show. "It was such a scarlet letter to me. It always felt like it was just less than everybody else. So I wanted that validation of having a scholarship. It meant more to me when I finally got it."

So he tore it off. Doering walked on for Steve Spurrier in 1991 and had a scholarship before his sophomore season. Nobody gave it to him. He took it, one scout-team rep at a time. Then he went out and rewrote the Florida record book.

He left in 1995 with 31 touchdown catches, still the school record and second in SEC history. Think about the receivers who have come through Gainesville since then. None of them has caught him.

He finished with 149 catches for more than 2,000 yards. His senior season was something special: 70 catches, 1,045 yards and 17 touchdowns. That earned him second-team All-America from The Associated Press and first-team All-SEC from both the league's coaches and the AP. The 17 scores still rank second on Florida's single-season list.

Doering wasn't a passenger, either. He helped the Gators win three straight SEC titles from 1993 to 1995. Jacksonville drafted him in the sixth round in 1996, and he lasted 10 seasons in the NFL with Indianapolis, Denver, Washington and Pittsburgh.

Ten years is a long time for a guy they once said was too slow and too small and not on scholarship.

The Phone Call

The best part of this story isn't the stats. It's the phone call. Last summer, Florida SID Scott Burns called Doering. He said coach Jon Sumrall wanted to know whether Doering would be doing his show in Atlanta for SEC Championship weekend, and whether he'd speak to the team the Friday night before the game.

Doering admits his first thought was a raised eyebrow. "I'm thinking, 'Man, first year, they're already ambitious enough to believe they're going to be in the SEC Championship Game?'" he said. "I was like, 'Sure, I'll be happy to do it.' I figured we'd cross that bridge when we got there."

A few weeks later, with Florida in preseason camp, Burns called back. He wanted to "run something past" Doering, Tuesday at 2:35. The phone rang. Doering picked up and said, "What's up, Scott?"

It wasn't Scott. "Hey, this is actually Coach Sumrall. They talked football for a few minutes, the camp and what the staff was seeing. Then Sumrall told him why he'd really called. "He goes, 'Well, sorry to mislead you, but we just wanted to break the news to you that you're going to be the legend representative for the Gators when we go to SEC Championship weekend,'" Doering said.

"I was almost in tears just hearing him say that. To have him take the time during training camp to deliver that news to me really made it even more special."

Give Sumrall credit. A first-year head coach in the middle of camp has a hundred things to do. He stopped to make that call himself, and that tells you he understands what Florida football is supposed to mean.

What Kept Him Going

As for the scout team, people don't know how punishing it is. Every walk-on has two or three days when you're ready to quit, beat up, ignored and wondering why you're doing it. Doering didn't quit. I asked him what kept him going.

"Couple things stand out to me, Buddy," he said. "One, we have this ignorance in life, some naivety, we'll call it. Luckily, we never know how hard the journey's going to be. Because if we knew in advance how hard it was going to be, we probably wouldn't sign up for it, you know?

"So I didn't know what I was getting into. I believed in myself, and my parents supported me as a walk-on, paying for my school and housing and everything else. And so I just did it.

"And the luck that I had in playing for Coach Spurrier, who didn't care if you were a walk-on or a scholarship player. He just wanted guys to compete and do the things they were coached to do. So I was just lucky with the timing of all of it." Lucky? Maybe a little.

But luck doesn't get you through a year of getting knocked flat by scholarship players while your parents pay the rent. Even after he made it, the road kept turning on him.

He became a hero at Kentucky, led the conference in catches a couple of weeks later, then landed in Spurrier's doghouse and lost his playing time for the rest of the season. He had to earn his way back again.

"It's never a direct path," Doering said. "Success takes longer and is more of a convoluted path. But at the end, the sacrifice you make and the work you put in makes it that much more gratifying."

Some people have asked him why this honor took so long. He doesn't see it that way.

"There's hundreds of players every single year on this team," he said. "There's way better players than I am that still haven't been recognized. … So I'm just grateful to have the honor."

That's how a former walk-on thinks, even 30 years later.

The Last One

Now for the part that hurts. "We're about to be in the last SEC Championship that we'll ever have," Doering said.

With playoff expansion coming, he believes this December's game in Atlanta will be the final one. For those of us who watched it grow, that's hard news.

Florida built that game. Spurrier, Wuerffel, Doering and a whole line of Gator All-Americans left their mark on it. The idea that it could disappear is devastating to all of them, and to me.

I reminded him of something Spurrier often says and Nick Saban said not long ago: for teams in the South, winning the SEC meant more than winning the national championship. That was certainly true in Florida.

Doering was there at the beginning. He played in the first four.

"At the inception of the SEC Championship Game in '92, when we went to Birmingham, we were like, 'What is this?'" he said. "We had no idea what it was. It quickly became the original conference championship game. Nobody ever did it as good as the SEC did, especially when we moved to Atlanta and what it became. "It does mean more. I would say now you have a better chance of winning a national championship than you do an SEC championship, with only two teams making it. It's a very huge honor to even play in that game."

If he's right about this year, the timing is almost too neat. A guy who was there at the start will be honored at the finish. The legend class will be celebrated Dec. 4 at the SEC Legends Celebration presented by T-Mobile at the College Football Hall of Fame in Atlanta. The honorees will be recognized again Dec. 5 before the SEC Championship Game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. 'Doering's Got a Touchdown!'

No Gator fan will ever forget the night of Sept. 11, 1993, in Lexington. Florida's quarterbacks threw seven interceptions that night. The Gators trailed Kentucky 20-17 with seconds left. Then redshirt freshman Danny Wuerffel fired a 28-yard pass over the middle to the former walk-on, and Mick Hubert lost his mind on the radio:

"DOERING'S GOT A TOUCHDOWN! DOERING'S GOT A TOUCHDOWN! OHHHH MYYYY!"

Florida won 24-20 with three seconds to play. Doering has said that catch "changed the trajectory of my life." It also helped launch a run of four straight SEC titles.

Plenty of players arrive at Florida with five stars and a scholarship. Chris Doering arrived with nothing but stubbornness.

They gave him a scout-team jersey and expected him to disappear, and in December he's going to Atlanta as a legend. Doering's got a touchdown! Again. Make that "The Legend's Got A Touchdown!"

posts.title: Gator Football Feel-Good: The Open Date Is Sweet Music, But Check the Lyrics
posts.description: Buddy Martin on Florida's open date, the lessons of past bye weeks and the Oct. 31 Georgia matchup in Atlanta. Photo by Chris Spears, GatorBait Media.
posts.author: Buddy Martin
posts.html:
By Buddy Martin

Photo by Chris Spears, GatorBait Media.

Two words on a football schedule don't mean much to most people: "Open Date." To a normal citizen it's a blank square on the calendar. It's a fine Saturday for a wedding, a trip to the mountains or finally cleaning the gutters.

But if your life is built around a football team, those two words sound like a Merle Haggard ballad drifting out of a jukebox. Sweet, a little sad and exactly what you needed to hear.

For Jon Sumrall, this week is that song.

His Gators have played seven straight Saturdays. They've been to the mountaintop, No. 8 in the country after running Ole Miss out of the Swamp 52-28.

They've been in the ditch beside it, falling out of the poll after a homecoming loss to South Carolina. Then last weekend they went to Austin, where the barbecue smoke hangs over the interstate and nobody expects the visitors to leave happy, and beat No. 7 Texas 27-24.

That's a season's worth of mood swings in seven weeks. A team needs a nap.

So this Saturday in Gainesville, the practice fields will be quiet and the training room will be full. It'll be ice tubs instead of film sessions. Somewhere a backup linebacker will sleep until noon and call it the best thing to happen to him since signing day.

Florida is 5-2, ranked No. 20 and back in the conversation. That's the cheerful part.

Now for the part where I squint.

In their infinite wisdom, the voters put Texas at No. 19, one spot ahead of the Gators. That's the team Florida just beat on its own field. It's like losing the wrestling match and getting the trophy anyway because your singlet fit better.

I've been reading polls longer than some of those voters have been alive, and I still can't tell you what they're measuring.

Apparently neither can Mario Cristobal, but more on him in a minute.

The History of Doing Nothing

Open dates get oversold, like a waterfront lot in Florida that comes with alligators.

Rest heals, but rest also rusts.

Look at 1996, the gold standard of Gator football. Steve Spurrier's national champions had three open dates that season: Sept. 14, Oct. 26 and Nov. 23.

Coming off the first, they went to Knoxville and beat No. 2 Tennessee 35-29. Coming off the second, they beat Georgia 47-7. Coming off the third, they went to Tallahassee and lost to Florida State 24-21 — due mostly to two regular offensive linemen being injured and out. And don't get me started on the late hits to "the echo of the whistle" by FSU.

So the most famous rest-week record in Gator history is 2-1, and the one blemish on a national champion came right after a week off.

Steve Spurrier got his revenge in the Sugar Bowl, 52-20, for the natty. As he put it, "we won the one that really counted the most." But that November, nobody in Gainesville was calling open dates magic.

The lesson then is the lesson now: the week off doesn't win anything. Depth does. A rested team with nobody behind the starters is just a team that's about to get tired again.

Florida has been on the other end of the calendar math, too. In 2019, the Gators and Miami opened in Week 0 in Orlando. That stretched a 12-game schedule over 15 weeks and gave Florida three open dates. Good teams use that kind of breathing room. Thin teams just get more time to worry.

Meanwhile, Down in Coral Gables

Here's where the record skips.

The same week Florida climbed back into the Top 25, guess who's sitting on top of it?

The Miami Hurricanes are No. 1 in the AP poll for the first time since Dec. 8, 2002. A whole generation of Canes fans had never seen it. Some only knew about it from uncles in gold chains.

They got there the hard way and the easy way at once. The hard way was a 43-35 double-overtime escape against Florida State. The easy way was No. 1 Georgia losing at home to unranked Auburn 27-24 while No. 2 Notre Dame lost at BYU.

Five of the top seven teams went down on one Saturday, a first in poll history.

Miami won the No. 1 ranking the way you win a hot-dog eating contest after everybody else gets sick.

To his credit, Cristobal isn't buying the crown. He called the ranking "absolutely insignificant and irrelevant with the changing of the guard from week to week." He's right. Texas held No. 1 and lost to unranked Oklahoma. Georgia took over and lost to unranked Auburn. In 2026, the top spot has been less a throne than a trap door.

Miami gets unranked Pitt this week. History says the Hurricanes should check the floorboards.

The Real Reason to Rest

Here's my footnote to the cheerful news. Florida's open date isn't exactly a head start, because Georgia is off this week, too. The two teams meet Oct. 31 in Atlanta. Not Jacksonville, which still feels like a priest saying Mass in a bowling alley. Both will arrive with fresh legs and fresh grudges.

The wise guys favor the Bulldogs by 12.5 points, with the over/under at 53.5. The same Bulldogs who lost to Auburn last week. Auburn, of course, was one of the five teams the Gators had beaten this year, but put that aside for right now.

Georgia will be angry about Auburn, and Florida will be confident about Austin. The Bulldogs' staff will spend the week reminding the players how that loss felt. Sumrall will spend it hoping his players' ankles heal faster than their egos swell.

That's the job of an open date. It isn't for celebrating the last win; it's for getting ready for the next fight. Heal the ankles. Fix the pass protection. Remind the young guys that No. 20 is a number, not a résumé.

So enjoy the quiet Saturday, Gator Nation. Go to the wedding, take the trip, clean the gutters.

Just be back by Halloween. The music's about to get loud again.

posts.title: Jones vs. Philo and other QB perceptions, realities
posts.description: Franz Beard examines quarterback recruiting hype, Florida's Aaron Philo–Tramell Jones Jr. decision and the history of the Gators' five-star quarterbacks.
posts.author: Franz Beard
posts.html:
Cover photo courtesy UAA and Hannah White.

Nowhere in collegiate sports are the expectations higher than they are for quarterbacks tagged with a fifth star, most often by a recruiting analyst who might have been a star in the co-ed intramural flag football league back in the day. Five stars projects the perception of greatness even before the first collegiate snap is taken. It also projects the greatest perception of bust for those who don't measure up to expectations that range from stratospheric to walks on water.

Talent alone is no guarantor for success at quarterback, where borderline insane expectations have to deal with the reality of the greatest risk and overall the fewest rewards. Nationally since 2015 there have been 38 quarterbacks with a 5-star rating (per 247Sports) of which it could be said that seven performed up to or beyond expectations. The two 5-stars signed by the Florida Gators during that span – Feleipe Franks and DJ Lagway – had pockets of success before transferring out.

The quarterback under the most scrutiny at present and perhaps since some keyboard cowboy came up with star ratings is Arch Manning, described as a generational talent when he signed with Texas in 2023. After sitting two years while backing up Quinn Ewers, another 5-star whose career never matched expectations, Manning is 16-4 as the starter but very few of the winning starts have earned spectacular reviews. Three of the four losses are to unranked teams including a pair of blemishes at the hands of Florida.

It really isn't fair to compare Arch Manning with his Hall of Fame heritage – grandfather Archie and uncles Peyton and Eli – particularly in light of Texas coach Steve Sarkisian's track record with quarterback development. Quinn Ewers was also described as a generational talent but his 27-9 record as the starting QB under Sarkisian left both the fan base and nation asking overhyped or undercoached? The same questions are being asked of Arch Manning, still the No. 1 QB at Texas even though Sarkisian is giving some first team reps to freshman KJ Lacey.

At Florida, where the quarterback position has produced three Heisman Trophy winners, eight have arrived since 2000 with 5-star ratings. Only two – Chris Leak and Tim Tebow – have proven worthy of the hype. Cam Newton also lived up to the hype but only after transferring to juco and then to Auburn. Those three have national championship rings to validate their 5-star ratings.

The most recent 5-star at Florida was DJ Lagway, who arrived in 2024 as the nation's No. 1 recruit. As a part-time starter in 2024 and full-time in 2025 he produced a 10-9 record and barely more touchdowns (28) than interceptions (23). Lagway is at Baylor now where his scattergun accuracy is creating calls for his benching in favor of Nate Bennett, a borderline 3-star when he arrived from a California high school in 2024.

There is no quarterback controversy at Florida currently where neither Aaron Philo nor Tramell Jones Jr. were anything close to 5-stars coming out of high school. Philo, a former 3-star recruit at Georgia Tech, started Florida's first six games (4-2 record) but an injury to the AC joint in his right (throwing) shoulder opened the door for Jones (former 4-star) to start last week against Texas, where he played turnover-free to beat the then 7th-ranked Longhorns and Manning in his first collegiate start. If Philo's injury lingers and Jones has continued success, it will force head coach Jon Sumrall to make a tough decision when Philo is healthy. Will he stick with the unwritten football rule that you don't lose your starting job to an injury or will he stick with the QB who is winning since taking over the job?

From a statistical and experience standpoint, Philo has the better track record but Jones, of course, hasn't had the opportunities. The one thing that Jones does have over Philo is a comeback win. Jones brought the Gators back from a 17-3 deficit to beat Texas in Austin and while his stats were quite average, they don't take into account inspiration. The troops responded to Jones. The two previous weeks against Missouri and South Carolina Philo was unsuccessful in rallying the troops to mount a comeback. How will that factor into a starting QB decision when Philo is healthy to play again?

The only one who can answer that question is Sumrall who says he is confident the Gators can win with either Philo or Jones taking the snaps. There is no quarterback controversy at Florida now, but that's not to say it will hold true a couple of weeks from now.
